Mahler-measure norm argument at measure two

Words: 86
Mahler measure OurBigBook.com
Let an irreducible f∈Z[X] have M(f)=2 and a root outside the closed unit disk. Its leading coefficient must have absolute value one. The product B of all roots outside the unit disk is then an algebraic integer with ∣B∣=2; conjugate pairs make B real, so B=±2. The quotient of the norm of any root by B is both rational and an algebraic integer, and its absolute value is at most one. It is therefore ±1, so every root has absolute norm two.

If gcd(a,b)=1 and a∣bc in a greatest-common-divisor domain, then a∣c. Indeed, the least common multiple of a and b is associate to ab and divides every common multiple; applying this to bc and cancelling b proves the claim.

Every complex number is within squared distance at most 3/4 of an Eisenstein integer: write it as x+yω and round x and y to integers. Therefore, for nonzero β and arbitrary α, a nearest lattice point q to α/β gives

Commutative algebra OurBigBook.com

F(X)=an​Xn+⋯+a0​∈Z[X],
(214)
if a prime p does not divide an​, divides every aj​ for j<n, and has p2∤a0​, then F is irreducible. If F=GH, reduction modulo p forces both G and H to be positive-degree monomials.
